**Try the live demo** to pan, zoom, focus, and export a sample schema in your browser, no install needed, then build a palette in the **theme builder** and copy the config. See what has shipped and what is next on the **roadmap**.

To use Truss in a non-local environment you must both enable it and authorize the viewers. See Authorization.

It exits `0` when clean, `1` when a finding is at or above the `--fail-on` level (default `error`), and `2` on a bad option or a snapshot error, so a migration that introduces a problem can fail the build. Presets (`recommended`, `strict`, `none`), per-rule severity and enable / disable, ignore patterns, and the fail level are all configurable under `truss.doctor`. See the configuration reference.
Every finding carries a stable code (e.g. `TRUSS-IDX-001`) shown in both the command and the panel; the schema doctor guide lists all the rule codes and what each checks.

If your project uses Laravel Boost, Truss ships guidelines and a skill that Boost finds on its own, so an agent set up through Boost knows Truss is installed and reaches for your real schema. There is no MCP server to wire up by hand for this path.
|**MCP server**|The richest surface: five tools and a resource, queried on demand, always current|`composer require laravel/mcp`, then point your client at `php artisan mcp:start truss`|
|**Laravel Boost**|The lowest friction if you already use Boost, across every agent Boost configures|`php artisan boost:install`, tick Truss|
|**`truss:export`**|CI, scripts, and any CLI-capable agent; no optional dependency at all|None, it ships with Truss|

The commands take the same options as their artisan counterparts and run the same code, so the text exports and the doctor report are byte-identical to what artisan prints. The exit codes match too: `0` clean, `1` doctor findings at the fail level or export drift with `--check`, and `2` for anything else, including a bad connection string, an unreachable host, an unknown option, or a PHP older than 8.2. An unreachable database can never be read as a schema with problems. The full reference is on the docs site.
Prefer to design it visually? The **theme builder** lets you dial in colours and fonts against a live dashboard preview and copy the config block straight into `config/truss.php`.

Truss exposes structure only and never queries row data. Access is protected by the fixed `viewTruss` gate. The standalone binary has no gate: there is no route to protect, and whoever runs it already holds the database credentials. It reads structure only, like the package, and its error messages never contain the connection string. If you discover a security issue, please email hello@albertoarena.it rather than opening a public issue.

Using Filament? albertoarena/filament-truss puts this diagram inside your admin, as a page rather than a frame around the dashboard. It is built from the panel's own components and takes the panel's own theme, so a custom panel needs no configuration. Access follows Truss, not the panel: `truss.enabled` first, then the `viewTruss` gate outside `local`, so being let into the admin is not on its own permission to read the structure. The guide is at trussphp.com/filament.

The Steampipe Postgres Foreign Data Wrapper (FDW) is a Postgres extension that translates APIs to foreign tables. It does not directly interface with external systems, but instead relies on plugins to implement API- or provider-specific code that returns data in a standard format via gRPC. See the Writing Plugins guide to get started writing Steampipe plugins.

The FDW is part of the Steampipe project. Bundled with the Steampipe CLI, it works with one or more of the plugins you install in Steampipe. You can also install one or more plugin-specific extensions in your own instance of Postgres.
To use the FDW with Steampipe, download Steampipe and use it to install one or more plugins.

- Multi-Threaded Command Processing - Commands in the queue are handled in multiple threads for faster processing.
- Reconfigurable Command Privileges - The user privileges required to execute commands can be completely reconfigured.

You must be wondering, how on earth do you play a game entirely in MariaDB. Well, it is simple. The entire game is played with stored procedures. Yes, I'm being serious. Every command must start with `CALL`, case-insensitive, and end with a semi-colon. For example: `CALL help;`.
* For locations, like stations, that contain multiple possibilities, the first arg will designate the specific numerical location.
* Example: `CALL grill_put(2, 'raw_beef');` will put raw_beef at grill station 2.
* For locations, like stations, that contain multiple possibilities, the arg will designate the specific numerical location.
* Example: `CALL storage_take('raw_beef');` Will take a raw beef from the kitchen storage and add it to the player's inventory.
- `read_one(query, *args, as: MyClass)`: asserts that one and only one row matches your query. If there are 0 or >1, an exception is raised.
- `read_one?(query, *args, as: MyClass)`: returns either the first matching row or `nil` if no rows match.
- `read_all(query, *args, as: MyClass) : Array(MyClass)`: returns all matching rows as an array
- `write_one(query, *args, as: MyClass)`: asserts a single match, assumes a `RETURNING` clause
- `write(query, *args)`: runs the specified query and ignores any returned data

> **Status:** early, in production at KeepPlain, our own Laravel SaaS on Postgres, where LokaDB started. LokaDB works with any application that talks to Postgres over its protocol, in any language and with any ORM: only the connection string changes. What decides is your schema and your queries, not the framework, and `lokadb check` tells you before anything is changed. Every build is tested end to end under load with three unmodified applications (Laravel, Django, Go) and against more than 300 failure scenarios. See What's supported, Limits and the roadmap.

|`fdw`|every statement goes to the cloud Postgres, which reads the organization through `postgres_fdw`|the organization is close to the cloud, or the workload joins its tables with cloud tables a lot|

|`fdw+direct` (default when direct credentials are configured)|statements that touch only this organization's tables go straight to its database; the rest go through `postgres_fdw`|the usual choice for a remote organization|
|`direct`|no `postgres_fdw` path at all; the cloud database holds no credentials for the organization|the application names the organization itself (cooperative mode)|
**In the browser.** the online demo runs a demo stand: a cloud database, organizations in their own databases, a demo application, and the compatibility report — nothing to install.

**Locally, with Docker.** One command starts a cloud Postgres, one organization's Postgres behind the relay and the agent, the proxy, and a small application that keeps writing for two organizations; it then runs `check`, `enable` and `move-org` and shows where each organization's rows ended up (Quickstart). It is a demo on throwaway databases; to put LokaDB in front of your own, see Install on your database. Run it from the root of this repository:
The full test stand — three applications and several hundred end-to-end and defect checks — is `bash e2e/run.sh` (see Testing).
The main steps, each of which can be stopped and undone. Install on your database has every command in full, and says which machine runs it.

|1. Check|`lokadb check -db DSN -org-table TABLE -write-spec spec.json -workload workload.json`|Reads the schema, the workload the proxy recorded (`lokadb proxy -record`, see the install page) and, later, the organization's database, and reports what blocks the move, what LokaDB does not support yet, and what will behave differently. Changes nothing.|

|2. Enable|`lokadb enable -db DSN -spec spec.json -owner ROLE`|Converts the chosen tables to partitioned tables in place (online preparation with `enable -prepare` for large tables). All organizations stay in the cloud.|

|3. Connect|`lokadb relay -config relay.json`; `lokadb token -cp DSN -org 1`, then `lokadb agent …` in the organization's network|A relay in your network and an agent in the organization's: the agent opens the only connection, outbound, with a one-time token.|

|4. Move|`lokadb move-org -db DSN -spec spec.json -owner ROLE -org 1 -customer DSN -customer-app DSN -proxy-config proxy.json -direct-role ROLE`|Moves one organization to its own database while the application keeps writing. At the switch-over the reads and writes of **all** organizations on the moved tables pause — seconds for an organization tens of milliseconds away (see Performance).|

|5. Profile|`lokadb org-profile -db DSN -org 1 fdw+direct`|Chooses how the proxy reaches that organization. `move-org` already picks `fdw+direct` when the proxy has the direct path's credentials; this switches later.|
|6. Back|`lokadb move-back -db DSN -spec spec.json -org 1 -customer DSN`|Returns the organization to the cloud; `lokadb disable` then undoes `enable`.|

The application only changes its connection string to point at the proxy (`host`, `port`). Relations your schema does not declare as foreign keys (common in Rails and Laravel), cross-organization reports and background jobs need a decision from you: `lokadb check` lists every such query with the reason no organization was found, and you declare the missing relations in the spec (`routing.relations`) or allow the reviewed reports. See Compatibility check and Routing.

**Scale:** one partition per organization. Up to about 100 organizations there is no noticeable price; at 1000 throughput is lower (reads and updates by a third to a half, inserts by about a third) and at 3000 inserts fall to about 1,400 ops/s, so we do not recommend mixed writes at that scale yet. Details and the mechanism in Limits and isolation.
The full list, and what is planned, is in Roadmap and Limits and isolation.

Measured on seven separate servers, not in Docker on one machine: a cloud database (8 cores, 32 GB), the proxy together with the relay (4 cores, 16 GB), a load generator (4 cores, 16 GB), and the databases of four organizations (2 cores, 4–8 GB each) at 0.19, 9.4, 38.7 and 43.3 ms round-trip time from the cloud. Postgres 18, `fsync` on, one scenario at a time; every point is 60 s after 15 s of warm-up, two repeats, the median. All figures are **for this workload** — access by primary key and by an `(organization_id, id)` index; another workload gives other numbers. Method, scenarios and raw results are in `research/bench/`; the numbers behind every chart are in charts-data.md.
Cost of the proxy for organizations that stay in the cloud
Requests per second with a new connection for every request

**A moved organization** pays for distance: its latency is almost linear in the round-trip time. At 43 ms a read through `fdw` takes 352 ms and through `fdw+direct` 133 ms; an update 351 and 89 ms. The same page has the ceilings by number of clients and of organizations, the pause of a move and the load limit: Performance. Where the round trips come from and what to tune is explained there too.

- **Not an authorization layer.** If the application asks for another organization's document by id, the proxy routes the query to where that document lives. Who may read what is still the application's job. The cross-tenant suite tries to reach another organization's rows in the awkward shapes, and says what it does not promise.

- **What LokaDB does not isolate:** your application's caches, queues, search indexes, files, logs and error reports; backups and replicas made before the move; values sampled into the cloud's Postgres statistics; and, on the `fdw` profile, the moved rows in transit through the cloud Postgres (memory, temporary files, logs if `log_statement` is on). The full list is in Limits and isolation; promise customers isolation only together with that list.
Report vulnerabilities as described in the security policy.

LokaDB is under active development by a small team. The core — `check`, `enable`, the proxy, `move-org`, the way back, migrations, the tunnel — is complete for the supported scope and is covered by an end-to-end stand and a suite of regression checks for every defect found so far. It runs in production at KeepPlain, our own Laravel SaaS on Postgres, where it started. What is next is in the Roadmap.

pi-oracle sends project files and questions from Pi to ChatGPT or Grok through your web account. Each job uses an isolated browser and saves its answer locally.
Oracle workflow: Pi packages project files, an isolated browser sends them to ChatGPT or Grok, and Oracle saves the answer locally.
Install `agent-browser` and `tar`. Install `zstd` for ChatGPT jobs. Check the platform requirements for the Node.js minimum, profile copies, and encrypted cookies.
Sign in to ChatGPT in your source browser profile. Your account must have access to the selected preset.
|`/oracle-auth [chatgpt\|grok]`|Import a provider login from your source browser profile.|
|`/oracle-read [job-id]`|Show status and a saved answer preview.|
|`/oracle-status [job-id]`|Show status and recent job ids when no explicit id is given.|
|`/oracle-clean <job-id\|all>`|Delete finished-job files. A recent notification can delay cleanup; retry at the time shown.|
By default, Oracle deletes completed and cancelled jobs after 14 days. It deletes failed jobs after 30 days. Copy files you need to keep. See retention settings for details.
ChatGPT accepts archives up to 250 MiB; Grok accepts up to 200 MiB. See providers and presets for archive formats, preset ids and model-picker limits.
Browser and authentication settings use the agent-level config. See configuration for project trust rules and custom cookie sources.
To update Oracle, run `pi update npm:pi-oracle`. See installation options for GitHub installs and other update commands.
